docs.syntax: =PROPER(TRIM(text)) tidies spacing and case; nest SUBSTITUTE and LOWER for a key
docs.explain:
TRIM removes padding at both ends of the text and collapses runs of spaces inside it to one. PROPER then capitalises the first letter of each word. Nested as PROPER(TRIM(A2)), they turn the padded, shouted name in A2 into Ana Lopez.

The order matters more than the functions do. PROPER applied to doubled spaces tidies the case and leaves the spaces in place, so the cleaned name still fails a lookup. MATCH does not ignore a trailing space, and it returns #N/A for a name that looks identical on screen.

The second screen builds a match key from the same text. TRIM goes first, SUBSTITUTE swaps the one remaining space for a dot, and LOWER flattens the case to ana.lopez. A key column is what lets two lists that spell a name differently join on one cell.

errors.text: A function is handed a whole range instead of one cell, which is not a single string to clean.
The function name is misspelled, and Excel returns #NAME?.
SUBSTITUTE runs before TRIM and every run of spaces becomes a run of dots in the key.

docs.atWork: An imported name column that has to match another list before anything joins to it.
docs.outcome: Tidy spacing and case with TRIM and PROPER, then build a lower-case key from the same text.
docs.teaches: TRIM before PROPER, then TRIM, SUBSTITUTE and LOWER nested into a match key
docs.dataset: Imported names with padding, doubled spaces and mixed case

screens.prompt: In B2, tidy the imported name in A2 so it has no stray spaces and each word is capitalised.

hints.syntax: =PROPER(TRIM(A2)): trim the spacing, then capitalise the words.
hints.func-trim: The cell is padded and doubled up, so the spaces go first.
hints.func-proper: Each word has to be capitalised rather than shouted.
hints.require-ref: The imported name is in A2.
hints.value: Padding and doubled spaces collapse, and the words become Ana Lopez.
hints.error: #VALUE! means the function was handed a whole range, which is not a single string to trim.

reject.why: the spacing is fixed but the name stays shouted
the padding and doubled spaces survive
neither the spacing nor the case is tidied
a trailing space is added back
the formula reads the second imported name rather than A2
the cleaned text is then divided by zero
the argument falls outside the parentheses

screens.prompt: In B2, build a lower-case key from the imported name in A2 with a dot where the space was.

hints.syntax: =LOWER(SUBSTITUTE(TRIM(A2)," ",".")): trim, replace the space, then lower-case.
hints.func-trim: Trim first, or the doubled spaces turn into doubled dots.
hints.func-substitute: The one space left between the names is swapped for a dot.
hints.func-lower: The name is shouted in the source, so the key is lower-cased.
hints.require-ref: The imported name is in A2, at the top of the column.
hints.value: Ana Lopez becomes ana.lopez once the padding is gone.
hints.error: If the key comes out with two dots, SUBSTITUTE ran before TRIM rather than after it.

reject.why: the key is built but never lower-cased
the space is left as a space
the padding and doubled spaces never leave the string
a hyphen is not the separator the key needs
the formula reads the second imported name rather than A2
the key is then divided by zero
the argument falls outside the parentheses

seo.title: Clean up an imported list in Excel
seo.description: TRIM removes padding and collapses doubled spaces, then PROPER fixes the case. That order matters, and the tidied name is what lets a later lookup match.
